title: TLS
subtitle: How TLS 1.3 achieves 1-RTT handshakes, forward secrecy via ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, X.509 chains, and mutual TLS (mTLS).
keyTakeaways: TLS combines asymmetric cryptography for initial authentication and key exchange with symmetric cryptography for high-speed payload encryption.
TLS 1.3 cuts connection latency to 1-RTT (or 0-RTT on resumption) by removing legacy cipher negotiations and mandating ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE).
Mutual TLS (mTLS) enforces zero-trust architecture across internal microservices by requiring both client and server to verify each other's X.509 certificates.
architectureDiagram:
TLS 1.3 HANDSHAKE (1-RTT Setup)
Client --- ClientHello (Key Share: ECDHE) -----------------> Server
Client <-- ServerHello + Certificate + Finished (Key Share) - Server
[ Symmetric Session Keys Generated Locally on Both Ends ]
Client --- Finished + Encrypted HTTP Request -------------> Server (Data flow)

sections.heading: Hybrid Cryptography and the TLS 1.3 Speedup
sections.body: Asymmetric cryptography (RSA, ECC) provides secure identity verification and key exchange across untrusted networks, but encrypting bulk data with asymmetric keys is computationally prohibitive. Symmetric cryptography (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) encrypts gigabytes of data per second with minimal CPU load, but requires both parties to share a secret key beforehand. TLS resolves this by using asymmetric key exchange to agree on a temporary symmetric session key, which encrypts all subsequent traffic.
bullets: TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3: TLS 1.2 required two round trips (2-RTT) for cipher negotiation and key exchange. TLS 1.3 cuts this to a single round trip (1-RTT) by guessing the key exchange group upfront.

Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE): Generates one-time session keys that are discarded after connection close, guaranteeing Forward Secrecy. Even if a server's private key is leaked in the future, past recorded traffic cannot be decrypted.

0-RTT Resumption (Early Data): Allows clients reconnecting to a known server to send encrypted HTTP requests in the first packet, though vulnerable to replay attacks unless guarded by anti-replay caches.

sections.heading: Mutual TLS (mTLS) in Service Meshes
sections.body: Standard HTTPS authenticates only the server: the client verifies the server's certificate against a trusted public Certificate Authority (CA). In internal microservice architectures, perimeter-based security is insufficient. Mutual TLS (mTLS) requires both the client service and the server service to present valid X.509 certificates issued by a private internal CA (such as HashiCorp Vault or SPIFFE/Spire), guaranteeing authenticated identity and encrypted communication across every internal hop.
bullets: Zero-Trust Foundation: Prevents lateral movement inside a cluster if an attacker compromises a single container.
Cryptographic Service Identity: Certificates embed service identities (e.g., `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/payment-service`), enabling granular network policy enforcement.
Automated Rotation: Short-lived certificates (valid for 12-24 hours) rotate automatically in the background via sidecar proxies like Envoy.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple operation; universal browser and client library compatibility; zero client credential provisioning.
tradeOffs.cons: Authenticates only the server; backend services must rely on API keys or JWT tokens to identify callers.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Public-facing websites, mobile application backends, and external third-party API consumers.

tradeOffs.pros: Cryptographic client authentication at the network transport layer; defense-in-depth against insider threats and rogue containers.
tradeOffs.cons: Operational overhead of managing private PKI, automated certificate issuance, and rotation before expiration.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal microservice meshes (Envoy, Istio, Linkerd), financial payment gateways, and regulatory compliance zones.

interviewTip: Mention 'Forward Secrecy' when discussing TLS. Explain that by using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys (ECDHE) instead of static RSA key exchange, compromising a private certificate today does not allow an attacker to retroactively decrypt past intercepted network traffic.
